title: Why Do Psychiatric Disorders Persist in Humans?
gist: A large Nature Communications study finds that heritable psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, autism, and ADHD are genetically associated with specific forms of intelligence — reaction time, logical and pattern reasoning, and accumulated knowledge — in European populations, offering a possible resolution to why evolution has not purged these genes. The available text is the setup to an interview with study author Diego Londoño-Correa and stops before his answers.

insights.claim: Psychiatric conditions including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, autism, and ADHD are partially heritable yet debilitating, posing the paradox of why evolution has not eliminated genes that can jeopardize a person's ability to find a mate and have children.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Framing psychiatric genetics as a fitness paradox implies the associated alleles carry some compensating advantage, which reshapes how such genes should be interpreted in screening.
insights.quote: Why would evolution not eliminate the genes associated with a condition that can make life so difficult and even jeopardize one’s ability to find a mate and have children?

themes.theme: Intelligence disaggregated at the genetic level

insights.claim: A large Nature Communications study found that some psychiatric conditions are associated at the genetic level with specific forms of intelligence in European populations — reaction time, the ability to think logically and find patterns, and accumulated knowledge.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Genetic correlations between disorder risk and specific cognitive abilities complicate any simple 'select against disease alleles' logic in embryo screening.
insights.quote: some of these conditions are associated with specific forms of intelligence at the genetic level in European populations, such as reaction time, the ability to think logically and find patterns, as well as accumulated knowledge
insights.locator: Now a huge new study in Nature Communications

insights.claim: Earlier cognitive research into psychiatric conditions treated intelligence as a monolith, which obscured differences between individual cognitive traits and their distinct relationships to disorder risk.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: The finding only appears once a composite measure is decomposed — a general warning that aggregate indices can hide the signal researchers are hunting for.
insights.quote: Previous cognitive research into psychiatric conditions had treated intelligence as a monolith, which had obscured differences in individual cognitive traits.

insights.claim: The genetic link between psychiatric conditions and particular cognitive abilities presents a possible solution to the evolutionary puzzle of why psychiatric illness persists.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: If disorder-linked alleles ride along with valued cognitive traits, the tradeoff logic argues against expecting these conditions to disappear from the gene pool.
insights.quote: The findings present a possible solution to the evolutionary puzzle presented by psychiatric illness.
insights.locator: The findings present a possible solution

insights.claim: Study author Diego Londoño-Correa, a psychology graduate student at the University of Texas at Austin, connects these findings to the nature of intelligence, domestication syndrome in animals, and the dangers of designer baby genetics.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Flags embryo-selection services as the practical arena where trait-tradeoff genetics will be contested, though the article's text stops before the argument is made.
insights.quote: about what the findings tell us about the nature of intelligence, domestication syndrome in animals, and the dangers of designer baby genetics
insights.locator: I spoke with study author Diego Londoño-Correa
